topics.label: Introduction to the Initiation and Resolution of Inflammation
topics.groupedBecause: The lecturer welcomes the class and outlines how the session will integrate previously introduced immunological components to examine inflammatory reactions.

topics.label: Principles of Innate Immune Recognition
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics introduce the fundamental requirements and molecular strategies by which the innate immune system detects danger and discriminates self from non-self.

topics.label: Pattern Recognition Receptor Families and Inflammasomes
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics detail the major families of pattern recognition receptors, their compartmentalized signaling cascades, and the assembly of the inflammasome complex.

topics.label: Sentinel Cell Activation and Leukocyte Recruitment
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how activated tissue sentinel cells coordinate the multi-step extravasation and targeted migration of circulating leukocytes to the site of infection.

topics.label: Lymphatic Drainage and Antigen Transport
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic describes how dendritic cells leave inflamed tissue via the lymphatic system to present antigens in draining lymph nodes.

topics.label: Systemic Consequences of Excessive Inflammation
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic explores the life-threatening pathological complications that arise when localized inflammatory signaling spills over into systemic circulation.

topics.label: Mechanisms of Inflammatory Resolution
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic details the passive and active physiological processes that arrest immune activation and shut down acute inflammation.

topics.label: Tissue Repair, Chronic Inflammation, and Granuloma Formation
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics describe post-inflammatory wound healing and the persistence of non-resolving inflammatory states such as granulomas.

topics.label: Conclusion and Upcoming Topics
topics.groupedBecause: The lecturer wraps up the presentation and announces the subject of the subsequent lecture.
